blocks.en: The Sky That Will Not Stay Silent
blocks.es_reference: El Cielo que No Se Queda Callado

blocks.en: In the last unit we learned to follow the clues back to the Baker. In this unit we walk the first trail, and it begins by looking up. From the dawn of the human story, in every age and on every continent, men have lifted their eyes to the heavens and known, somewhere below words, that they were not alone. The African builds an altar to the sun. The Greek raises a statue to an unknown god, lest he overlook one. The modern man, who says he believes in nothing, stands in a hospital corridor at two in the morning and finds himself praying to a God he has not addressed in thirty years. Augustine put his finger on it: "You have made us for Yourself, and our hearts are restless until they rest in You." The longing is universal because the Maker is real, and He has not left Himself without a witness.
blocks.es_reference: En la unidad anterior aprendimos a seguir las pistas de vuelta al Panadero. En esta unidad recorremos el primer sendero, y comienza mirando hacia arriba. Desde el amanecer de la historia humana, en toda época y en todo continente, los hombres han alzado los ojos a los cielos y han sabido, en algún lugar debajo de las palabras, que no estaban solos. El africano levanta un altar al sol. El griego erige una estatua a un dios no conocido, no sea que pase uno por alto. El hombre moderno, que dice no creer en nada, está de pie en el pasillo de un hospital a las dos de la mañana y se encuentra orando a un Dios al que no se ha dirigido en treinta años. Agustín lo señaló: "Nos hiciste para Ti, y nuestro corazón está inquieto hasta que descanse en Ti." El anhelo es universal porque el Hacedor es real, y no se ha dejado a sí mismo sin testimonio.

blocks.en: This is why the psalmist says the fool has said in his heart, not in his head, "There is no God" (Psalm 14:1). Mark the place — the heart, not the head. Unbelief is far more often a wish than a conclusion. We do not see the wind, yet we believe in it without hesitation, because we see what it does: the bending tree, the driven cloud, the sail filled taut. So it is with God. We do not see Him with the eye, but we read His handiwork everywhere His wind has passed. Let us now follow that reading carefully.
blocks.es_reference: Por eso dice el salmista que el necio dijo en su corazón, no en su cabeza, "No hay Dios" (Salmo 14:1). Note el lugar — el corazón, no la cabeza. La incredulidad es mucho más a menudo un deseo que una conclusión. No vemos el viento, y sin embargo creemos en él sin vacilar, porque vemos lo que hace: el árbol que se dobla, la nube empujada, la vela tensa. Así es con Dios. No lo vemos con el ojo, pero leemos su obra dondequiera que ha pasado su viento. Sigamos ahora esa lectura con cuidado.

blocks.en: The Classical Scaffolding
blocks.es_reference: El Andamio Clásico

blocks.en: For centuries, thinking believers have offered a set of reasoned arguments for the existence of God. I want you to understand from the start what these arguments are and what they are not. They are not the house; they are the scaffolding. No man was ever argued into the kingdom by a syllogism, and these proofs will not by themselves give you a single saved soul. But scaffolding has its work: it lets the builder reach the wall. These arguments move an honest mind from "the universe is a random accident" to "the universe is a structured reality," and that is no small distance to travel. Five of them have stood the test of the centuries.
blocks.es_reference: Durante siglos, los creyentes pensantes han ofrecido un conjunto de argumentos razonados para la existencia de Dios. Quiero que entienda desde el principio qué son estos argumentos y qué no son. No son la casa; son el andamio. Ningún hombre fue jamás argumentado para entrar al reino por un silogismo, y estas pruebas no le darán por sí solas una sola alma salva. Pero el andamio tiene su obra: le permite al constructor alcanzar la pared. Estos argumentos mueven a una mente honesta de "el universo es un accidente al azar" a "el universo es una realidad estructurada", y esa no es poca distancia que recorrer. Cinco de ellos han resistido la prueba de los siglos.

blocks.en: First, the Argument from Cause
blocks.es_reference: Primero, el Argumento de la Causa

blocks.en: Everything that begins to exist has a cause; this is close to common sense, and it is the starting point of what philosophers call the cosmological argument. Picture a long line of dominoes, each one falling because the one before it fell. Trace the motion back: this one fell because that one struck it, and that one because the one before, and so on down the line. Defenders of this argument hold that a row of dominoes cannot fall on its own — that you cannot run the causes back forever, because an infinite regress does not by itself explain why anything is falling at all rather than nothing. Not every philosopher agrees that an infinite regress is impossible or explanatorily empty; the point has been debated for centuries. But for those who find the reasoning persuasive, it drives the mind toward a First Cause — itself uncaused, standing outside the chain, outside time and space, the One who pushed the first domino. "In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth."
blocks.es_reference: Todo lo que comienza a existir tiene una causa; esto se acerca al sentido común, y es el punto de partida de lo que los filósofos llaman el argumento cosmológico. Imagine una larga fila de fichas de dominó, cada una cayendo porque cayó la anterior. Siga el movimiento hacia atrás: esta cayó porque aquella la golpeó, y aquella por la anterior, y así por toda la fila. Quienes defienden este argumento sostienen que una fila de dominó no puede caer por sí sola — que no se pueden remontar las causas para siempre, porque un retroceso infinito no explica por sí mismo por qué algo está cayendo en absoluto en vez de nada. No todo filósofo está de acuerdo en que un retroceso infinito sea imposible o carezca de valor explicativo; el punto se ha debatido por siglos. Pero para quienes hallan persuasivo el razonamiento, este lleva la mente hacia una Primera Causa — ella misma sin causa, parada fuera de la cadena, fuera del tiempo y del espacio, Aquel que empujó la primera ficha. "En el principio creó Dios los cielos y la tierra."

blocks.en: Second, the Argument from Design
blocks.es_reference: Segundo, el Argumento del Diseño

blocks.en: William Paley gave us the picture that has never been bettered. Suppose, he said, you are walking across an open field and your foot strikes a stone. You think nothing of it; for all you know it has lain there forever. But suppose instead your foot strikes a watch. You pick it up and open the back, and there you find wheels within wheels, a coiled spring, jeweled bearings, hands sweeping in perfect order to mark the hour. You would never say this watch fell together by accident, or that the rain and the wind assembled it over time. The design demands a designer. Now lift your eyes from the watch to the eye that beholds it — the lens, the retina, the nerve, ten thousand parts in concert — or to the single living cell, more intricate than any city. As a watch implies a watchmaker, the design of the world implies a Designer.
blocks.es_reference: William Paley nos dio la imagen que nunca se ha superado. Suponga, dijo, que va caminando por un campo abierto y su pie tropieza con una piedra. No piensa nada de ello; por lo que sabe, ha estado allí desde siempre. Pero suponga en cambio que su pie tropieza con un reloj. Lo recoge y abre la tapa, y allí encuentra ruedas dentro de ruedas, un resorte enrollado, rubíes pulidos, manecillas que se mueven en orden perfecto para marcar la hora. Usted nunca diría que ese reloj se armó por accidente, ni que la lluvia y el viento lo ensamblaron con el tiempo. El diseño exige un diseñador. Ahora levante los ojos del reloj al ojo que lo contempla — el cristalino, la retina, el nervio, diez mil partes en concierto — o a la sola célula viva, más intrincada que cualquier ciudad. Como un reloj implica un relojero, el diseño del mundo implica un Diseñador.

blocks.en: Third, the Argument from Conscience
blocks.es_reference: Tercero, el Argumento de la Conciencia

blocks.en: There is a law written on the human heart, and every man knows it is there. Travel where you will, to any tribe or nation, and you will not find a people who honor cowardice or praise the betrayal of a friend. We may argue about the edges, but at the center every conscience says that cruelty is wrong and kindness is good — and says it not as a preference but as a command. Where does that "ought" come from? A law implies a lawgiver. If there is no God, then "wrong" means only "I happen to dislike it," and one man's dislike has no authority over another's. But we know better. When we cry out that an atrocity is evil, we are not announcing our taste; we are appealing to a standard above us both. That standard is the moral law, and behind the law stands the Lawgiver.
blocks.es_reference: Hay una ley escrita en el corazón humano, y todo hombre sabe que está allí. Viaje a donde quiera, a cualquier tribu o nación, y no hallará un pueblo que honre la cobardía o alabe la traición de un amigo. Podemos discutir sobre los bordes, pero en el centro toda conciencia dice que la crueldad es mala y la bondad es buena — y lo dice no como una preferencia sino como un mandato. ¿De dónde viene ese "deber"? Una ley implica un legislador. Si no hay Dios, entonces "malo" significa solo "no me gusta", y el disgusto de un hombre no tiene autoridad sobre el de otro. Pero sabemos que no es así. Cuando clamamos que una atrocidad es mala, no anunciamos nuestro gusto; apelamos a una norma por encima de ambos. Esa norma es la ley moral, y detrás de la ley está el Legislador.

blocks.en: Fourth, the Argument from Being
blocks.es_reference: Cuarto, el Argumento del Ser

blocks.en: This is the subtlest of the five, and I give it to you for your sharpest students. Anselm reasoned that God is the greatest being that can possibly be conceived. Now, he said, a being that exists in reality is greater than one that exists only in the mind. Therefore the greatest conceivable being must exist, for if He lacked existence He would not be the greatest. I will be honest with you about this one. The philosopher Immanuel Kant raised a famous objection — that existence is not a property we can add to a thing the way we add wisdom or power, and so we cannot define a being into reality. The argument has divided the finest minds for nine centuries, and we do not rest the case upon it. I offer it as the most rigorous of the five and I hold it humbly. A good apologist knows both the strength of his arguments and their limits.
blocks.es_reference: Este es el más sutil de los cinco, y se lo doy para sus estudiantes más agudos. Anselmo razonó que Dios es el mayor ser que se puede concebir. Ahora bien, dijo, un ser que existe en la realidad es mayor que uno que existe solo en la mente. Por tanto, el mayor ser concebible debe existir, porque si careciera de existencia no sería el mayor. Seré honesto con usted acerca de este. El filósofo Immanuel Kant levantó una objeción famosa — que la existencia no es una propiedad que podamos añadir a una cosa como añadimos la sabiduría o el poder, y por eso no podemos definir un ser hasta hacerlo real. El argumento ha dividido a las mentes más finas por nueve siglos, y no apoyamos el caso sobre él. Lo ofrezco como el más riguroso de los cinco y lo sostengo con humildad. Un buen apologista conoce tanto la fuerza de sus argumentos como sus límites.

blocks.en: Fifth, the Argument from Desire
blocks.es_reference: Quinto, el Argumento del Anhelo

blocks.en: C. S. Lewis gave this one its clearest form. Hunger does not prove that this particular man will get his dinner, but the existence of hunger does point to the existence of food. Thirst points to water; the wing points to air; the eye is made for light. Every native desire in us answers to some real object that can satisfy it. Yet there is one desire in the human heart that no food, no marriage, no success, no pleasure on this earth has ever filled — a homesickness for a country we have never seen. If we were made for this world only, why does nothing in this world content us? The likeliest answer is that we were made for Another, and the longing is the cord that ties us to Him.
blocks.es_reference: C. S. Lewis dio a este su forma más clara. El hambre no prueba que este hombre en particular vaya a recibir su cena, pero la existencia del hambre sí apunta a la existencia de la comida. La sed apunta al agua; el ala apunta al aire; el ojo está hecho para la luz. Todo deseo natural en nosotros responde a algún objeto real que puede satisfacerlo. Sin embargo, hay un deseo en el corazón humano que ninguna comida, ningún matrimonio, ningún éxito, ningún placer en esta tierra ha llenado jamás — una nostalgia por una patria que nunca hemos visto. Si fuéramos hechos solo para este mundo, ¿por qué nada en este mundo nos contenta? La respuesta más probable es que fuimos hechos para Otro, y el anhelo es el cordón que nos ata a Él.

blocks.en: The Goldilocks Zone
blocks.es_reference: La Zona de Ricitos de Oro

blocks.en: Now we come down from philosophy to the porridge that is "just right." When we examine the Earth, we find a planet remarkably well-suited for life. Consider the distance: ninety-three million miles from the sun, placing us within the range where water stays liquid — significantly closer and the oceans would eventually boil away; significantly farther and we would freeze into a permanent ice ball. Consider the tilt: twenty-three and a half degrees, and from that single angle come the seasons and the spreading of warmth across the globe. Consider the air: roughly twenty-one percent oxygen — scientists have observed that meaningfully higher oxygen concentrations would make wildfires far more severe and harder to extinguish, even in wet conditions, though the exact threshold is still studied and debated rather than fixed to a precise number. A thin layer of ozone holds back the deadly rays and lets the good light through.
blocks.es_reference: Ahora bajamos de la filosofía a la sopa que está "en su punto". Cuando examinamos la Tierra, hallamos un planeta notablemente bien adaptado para la vida. Considere la distancia: noventa y tres millones de millas del sol, colocándonos dentro del rango donde el agua se mantiene líquida — significativamente más cerca y los océanos eventualmente hervirían; significativamente más lejos y nos congelaríamos en una bola de hielo permanente. Considere la inclinación: veintitrés grados y medio, y de ese solo ángulo vienen las estaciones y el reparto del calor por el globo. Considere el aire: cerca del veintiuno por ciento de oxígeno — los científicos han observado que concentraciones de oxígeno significativamente más altas harían los incendios forestales mucho más severos y difíciles de apagar, incluso en condiciones húmedas, aunque el umbral exacto todavía se estudia y debate en vez de estar fijado a un número preciso. Una delgada capa de ozono contiene los rayos mortales y deja pasar la luz buena.

blocks.en: Nor is the Earth left to keep its balance alone. Our moon, by its size and distance, steadies the tilt of our world like a hand laid on a spinning top, so the seasons hold and the climate does not reel into chaos. And far out beyond us stands Jupiter, our great elder brother, three hundred times the mass of Earth. For decades astronomers popularized the idea that its vast gravity acts as a sentinel, drawing off comets and stones that might otherwise come our way; in 1994 we watched the comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 break apart and strike Jupiter, and many took this as confirmation of that shielding role. More recent studies have complicated the picture — some simulations show Jupiter's gravity also flings certain objects toward the inner solar system rather than only sweeping them away, so astronomers now debate its net effect on Earth's safety rather than treating it as settled. What is not disputed is that a comet of that size striking Earth would be a catastrophe of almost unimaginable scale. Shield or simply neighbor, the picture is much the same: it is as though the great house of the world was furnished and made ready for the guest before ever the guest arrived.
blocks.es_reference: Ni se deja a la Tierra guardar su equilibrio sola. Nuestra luna, por su tamaño y distancia, estabiliza la inclinación de nuestro mundo como una mano puesta sobre un trompo que gira, para que las estaciones se mantengan y el clima no se desplome en el caos. Y allá afuera, más allá de nosotros, está Júpiter, nuestro gran hermano mayor, trescientas veces la masa de la Tierra. Durante décadas los astrónomos popularizaron la idea de que su vasta gravedad actúa como un centinela, desviando cometas y piedras que de otro modo vendrían hacia nosotros; en 1994 vimos al cometa Shoemaker-Levy 9 partirse y golpear a Júpiter, y muchos lo tomaron como confirmación de ese papel protector. Estudios más recientes han complicado el panorama — algunas simulaciones muestran que la gravedad de Júpiter también lanza ciertos objetos hacia el sistema solar interior en vez de solo alejarlos, así que los astrónomos hoy debaten su efecto neto sobre la seguridad de la Tierra en vez de darlo por resuelto. Lo que no se discute es que un cometa de ese tamaño golpeando la Tierra sería una catástrofe de una escala casi inimaginable. Sea escudo o solo vecino, el cuadro es en gran parte el mismo: es como si la gran casa del mundo hubiera sido amueblada y preparada para el huésped antes de que el huésped llegara.

blocks.en: To the Door, but Not Yet Through It
blocks.es_reference: Hasta la Puerta, pero Aún No a Través de Ella

blocks.en: So the scaffolding stands, and the structure shows. The dominoes need a finger; the watch needs a maker; the law needs a giver; the longing has an object; the house was prepared for a guest. An honest mind, walking this trail, is brought a long way — from accident to design, from chaos to a structured reality. But remember what scaffolding is and is not. A structured universe is not yet a surrendered heart. These arguments can carry a man to the door and even make him lift his hand to knock. Who waits behind that door — the living God who does not merely leave fingerprints on the world but speaks within the soul — is the matter of our next unit. For now, let the wonder stand: could it be that all of this was made, and made for us, and made by One who wishes to be found?
blocks.es_reference: Así que el andamio está en pie, y la estructura se muestra. El dominó necesita un dedo; el reloj necesita un hacedor; la ley necesita un dador; el anhelo tiene un objeto; la casa fue preparada para un huésped. Una mente honesta, al recorrer este sendero, es llevada un largo trecho — del accidente al diseño, del caos a una realidad estructurada. Pero recuerde lo que el andamio es y no es. Un universo estructurado no es todavía un corazón rendido. Estos argumentos pueden llevar a un hombre hasta la puerta e incluso hacerlo levantar la mano para tocar. Quién espera detrás de esa puerta — el Dios vivo que no solo deja huellas sobre el mundo sino que habla dentro del alma — es el asunto de nuestra próxima unidad. Por ahora, deje que el asombro permanezca: ¿podría ser que todo esto fue hecho, y hecho para nosotros, y hecho por Uno que desea ser hallado?

blocks.en: "For since the creation of the world His invisible attributes are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made." — Romans 1:20
blocks.es_reference: "Porque las cosas invisibles de él, desde la creación del mundo, se ven claramente, siendo entendidas por las cosas que son hechas." — Romanos 1:20

sa.prompt: Explain the argument from cause (the cosmological argument) and the illustration the unit uses for it.
sa.model: The argument from cause, or cosmological argument, begins with the premise that everything that begins to exist has a cause. The unit pictures a long line of dominoes, each falling because the one before it fell. Defenders of the argument hold that we cannot trace the causes back forever, because an infinite regress does not by itself explain why anything is happening at all rather than nothing — though philosophers have long debated whether an infinite regress is truly impossible or explanatorily empty, so this premise is a piece of reasoning to be weighed, not a settled fact. For those who find it persuasive, reason drives toward a First Cause that is itself uncaused, standing outside the chain and outside time and space. That uncaused First Cause is what we call God, the One who pushed the first domino, as Genesis says, in the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.

sa.prompt: Explain Paley's argument from design (the teleological argument), including the watch illustration.
sa.model: The argument from design, or teleological argument, was given its clearest picture by William Paley. If you found a watch lying in a field, you would never say it had assembled itself by chance, because its wheels, spring, and moving hands show an order and complexity that demand a designer. The same is true of the eye, the living cell, and the intricate order of the world. As a watch implies a watchmaker, the design of creation implies a Designer. The point is not merely that the world is old or large, but that it is ordered and purposeful, and order of that kind does not arise from accident; it points beyond itself to a mind that made it.

sa.prompt: State the moral argument and explain why the universal sense of right and wrong points to a Lawgiver.
sa.model: The moral argument begins with the universal human sense of right and wrong. Across every tribe and nation we find that cruelty is condemned and kindness is praised, not merely as a preference but as something binding, a command. This points to a moral law written on the heart, and a law implies a Lawgiver. If there were no God, then 'wrong' would mean only that someone happens to dislike a thing, and one person's dislike would carry no authority over another's. But when we say an atrocity is truly evil, we appeal to a standard above us all. That objective standard is the moral law, and behind the law stands the transcendent Lawgiver who is God.

sa.prompt: Summarize the ontological argument (the argument from being) and the objection Kant raised against it.
sa.model: The ontological argument, framed by Anselm, defines God as the greatest being that can possibly be conceived. Anselm reasoned that a being existing in reality is greater than one existing only in the mind, so the greatest conceivable being must exist, since otherwise it would not be the greatest. The unit treats this as the subtlest of the arguments. It also notes the famous objection of Immanuel Kant, who argued that existence is not a property we add to a thing the way we add wisdom or power, so we cannot simply define a being into reality. Because of this objection the unit holds the ontological argument humbly and does not rest the whole case upon it, offering it as the most rigorous of the five rather than as decisive proof.

sa.prompt: Explain the argument from desire (the argument from longing) as C. S. Lewis framed it.
sa.model: The argument from desire, given its clearest form by C. S. Lewis, observes that every natural desire answers to some real object that can satisfy it. Hunger does not prove a man will eat, but it points to the existence of food; thirst points to water, and the eye is made for light. Yet there is one longing in the human heart that nothing on this earth, no pleasure, no success, no relationship, has ever fully satisfied, a kind of homesickness for a country we have never seen. If we were made for this world alone, nothing in it should leave us so restless. The likeliest explanation is that we were made for God, and this deep, unsatisfied longing is the cord that ties the soul to its Maker.

sa.prompt: What does the unit mean by calling the classical arguments 'scaffolding, not the house'?
sa.model: The unit calls the classical arguments scaffolding, not the house. The point is that these proofs are not the saving faith itself; no one is argued into the kingdom by a syllogism. But scaffolding still has real work to do, because it lets the builder reach the wall. In the same way, the arguments move an honest mind from the assumption that the universe is a random accident to the recognition that it is a structured reality. They clear the ground and remove obstacles, taking a person from chaos to design. What they cannot do is produce a surrendered heart; that is the work of God's Spirit. So we use the scaffolding to prepare the way, and then we trust God to build the house.

sa.prompt: Describe the fine-tuning of the Earth (the 'Goldilocks' evidence) the unit presents.
sa.model: The unit describes the Earth as a planet remarkably well-suited for life, a Goldilocks world that is just right. It points to the distance from the sun, about ninety-three million miles, which places us within the range where water stays liquid — significantly closer and the oceans would eventually boil away, significantly farther and we would freeze into a permanent ice ball. It points to the axial tilt of about twenty-three and a half degrees, which gives us the seasons and spreads warmth across the globe. It points to the atmosphere, roughly twenty-one percent oxygen, a range well-suited for life, since scientists have observed that meaningfully higher levels would make wildfires far more severe and harder to extinguish, though the exact threshold is still studied and debated. And it points to the thin layer of ozone that holds back deadly rays while letting the good light through. Each of these is well-suited for life, even if the outer edges of just how narrow each window truly is remain subjects of ongoing scientific study.

sa.prompt: Explain the role the moon and Jupiter play in the fine-tuning case for life on Earth.
sa.model: The unit adds that the Earth does not keep its balance alone. The moon, by its size and distance, steadies the tilt of our world like a hand laid on a spinning top, so the seasons hold and the climate does not reel into chaos. Far beyond us stands Jupiter, three hundred times the mass of the Earth. For decades astronomers popularized the idea that its vast gravity acts as a sentinel, drawing off comets and asteroids that might otherwise strike us; the unit recalls that in 1994 the comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 struck Jupiter, which many took as confirmation of that shielding role. More recent research has complicated this picture, since some simulations show Jupiter's gravity also flings certain objects toward the inner solar system, so its net effect on Earth's safety is now debated among astronomers rather than settled. What is beyond dispute is that a comet of that size striking Earth would be a catastrophe of almost unimaginable scale. Shield or simply neighbor, the picture is much the same: a world prepared and provisioned for life.

sa.prompt: How does the universal longing for God across cultures serve as a witness to His reality?
sa.model: The unit observes that in every age and on every continent people have reached out for God, which it takes as a witness to His reality. It points to the universal longing Augustine named when he said our hearts are restless until they rest in God. It recalls cultures everywhere building altars and seeking the divine, even the Greeks raising an altar to an unknown god so as not to miss one, and the modern man who claims to believe nothing yet prays in a crisis. This widespread, restless seeking is hard to explain if there is nothing to seek. The simplest explanation is that the longing is universal because the Maker is real and has placed in every heart a homing instinct toward Himself.

sa.prompt: Why do the classical arguments bring a person 'to the door' but not through it?
sa.model: The unit ends by saying the classical arguments can bring a person to the door but cannot bring him through it. They can move an honest mind from accident to design and even make a man lift his hand to knock, but a structured universe is not yet a surrendered heart. The reason is that the last barrier is not in the mind but in the will, and reason alone cannot move the will. What is needed beyond the evidence is the work of God's Spirit, the living God who does not merely leave fingerprints on the world but speaks within the soul. So the apologist uses argument to clear the path to the door, and then trusts the Spirit to open it from the inside. This prepares the way for the next unit on the witness within.
